{{Short description|Square matrix which is its own inverse}}
In [[mathematics]], an '''involutory matrix''' is a [[square matrix]] that is its own [[inverse matrix|inverse]]. That is, multiplication by the matrix <math>\bold A_{n \times n}</math> is an [[Involution (mathematics)|involution]] if and only if <math> \bold A^2 = \bold I,</math> where <math>\bold I</math> is the <math>n \times n</math> [[identity matrix]]. Involutory matrices are all [[square root of a matrix|square roots]] of the identity matrix. This is a consequence of the fact that any [[invertible matrix]] multiplied by its inverse is the identity.<ref name="higham">{{citation
 | last = Higham | first = Nicholas J. | authorlink = Nicholas Higham
 | contribution = 6.11 Involutory Matrices
 | doi = 10.1137/1.9780898717778
 | isbn = 978-0-89871-646-7
 | location = Philadelphia, PA
 | mr = 2396439
 | pages = 165–166
 | publisher = Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM)
 | title = Functions of Matrices: Theory and Computation
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=2Wz_zVUEwPkC&pg=PA165
 | year = 2008}}.</ref>

== Examples ==
The <math>2\times2</math> [[real number|real]] matrix <math>\begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & -a \end{pmatrix}</math> is involutory provided that <math>a^2 + bc = 1 .</math><ref>[[Peter Lancaster]] & Miron Tismenetsky (1985) ''The Theory of Matrices'', 2nd edition, pp 12,13 [[Academic Press]] {{ISBN|0-12-435560-9}}</ref>

The [[Pauli matrices]] in {{tmath|M(2,\C)}} are involutory:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \sigma_1 = \sigma_x &=
    \begin{pmatrix}
      0 & 1 \\
      1 & 0
    \end{pmatrix}, \\
  \sigma_2 = \sigma_y &=
    \begin{pmatrix}
      0 & -i \\
      i & 0
    \end{pmatrix}, \\
  \sigma_3 = \sigma_z &=
    \begin{pmatrix}
      1 & 0 \\
      0 & -1
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{align}</math>

One of the three classes of [[elementary matrix]] is involutory, namely the row-interchange elementary matrix. A special case of another class of elementary matrix, that which represents multiplication of a row or column by −1, is also involutory; it is in fact a trivial example of a [[signature matrix]], all of which are involutory.

Some simple examples of involutory matrices are shown below.

<math display="block">
\begin{array}{cc}
\mathbf{I} = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}
; & 
\mathbf{I}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}
\\
\\
\mathbf{R} = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
; &
\mathbf{R}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\\
\\
\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix}
+1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -1
\end{pmatrix}
; &
\mathbf{S}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}
+1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & -1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -1
\end{pmatrix}
\\
\end{array}
</math>
where
* {{math|'''I'''}} is the 3 × 3 identity matrix (which is trivially involutory);
* {{math|'''R'''}} is the 3 × 3 identity matrix with a pair of interchanged rows;
* {{math|'''S'''}} is a [[signature matrix]].

Any [[block-diagonal matrix|block-diagonal matrices]] constructed from involutory matrices will also be involutory, as a consequence of the linear independence of the blocks.

== Symmetry ==
An involutory matrix which is also [[symmetric matrix|symmetric]] is an [[orthogonal matrix]], and thus represents an [[isometry]] (a [[linear transformation]] which preserves [[Euclidean distance]]). Conversely every orthogonal involutory matrix is symmetric.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Govaerts | first = Willy J. F.
 | doi = 10.1137/1.9780898719543
 | isbn = 0-89871-442-7
 | location = Philadelphia, PA
 | mr = 1736704
 | page = 292
 | publisher = Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics (SIAM)
 | title = Numerical methods for bifurcations of dynamical equilibria
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=rqvYq19qwiwC&pg=PA292
 | year = 2000}}.</ref>
As a special case of this, every [[Reflection (linear algebra)|reflection]] and 180° [[rotation matrix]] is involutory.

==Properties==
An involution is [[Defective matrix|non-defective]], and each [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalue]] equals <math>\pm 1</math>, so an involution [[diagonalizable matrix|diagonalizes]] to a signature matrix.

A [[Normal matrix|normal]] involution is [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]] (complex) or symmetric (real) and also [[Unitary matrix|unitary]] (complex) or orthogonal (real).

The [[determinant]] of an involutory matrix over any [[field (mathematics)|field]] is ±1.<ref name="bernstein">{{citation
 | last = Bernstein | first = Dennis S.
 | contribution = 3.15 Facts on Involutory Matrices
 | edition = 2nd
 | isbn = 978-0-691-14039-1
 | location = Princeton, NJ
 | mr = 2513751
 | pages = 230–231
 | publisher = Princeton University Press
 | title = Matrix Mathematics
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=-c0NxJg4vHMC&pg=PA230
 | year = 2009}}.</ref>

If {{math|'''A'''}} is an {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} matrix, then {{math|'''A'''}} is involutory if and only if <math>\bold P_+ = (\bold I + \bold A)/2</math> is [[Idempotent matrix|idempotent]]. This relation gives a [[bijection]] between involutory matrices and idempotent matrices.<ref name="bernstein"/> Similarly, {{math|'''A'''}} is involutory if and only if <math>\bold P_- = (\bold I - \bold A)/2</math> is [[Idempotent matrix|idempotent]].  These two operators form the symmetric and antisymmetric projections <math>v_\pm = \bold P_\pm v</math> of a vector <math>v = v_+ + v_-</math> with respect to the involution {{math|'''A'''}}, in the sense that <math>\bold Av_\pm = \pm v_\pm</math>, or <math>\bold{A P}_\pm = \pm \bold P_\pm</math>.  The same construct applies to any [[Involution (mathematics)|involutory function]], such as the [[complex conjugate]] (real and imaginary parts), [[transpose]] (symmetric and antisymmetric matrices), and [[Hermitian adjoint]] ([[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]] and [[Skew-Hermitian matrix|skew-Hermitian]] matrices).

If {{math|'''A'''}} is an involutory matrix in {{tmath|M(n, \R),}} which is a [[matrix algebra]] over the [[real number]]s, and {{math|'''A'''}} is not a scalar multiple of {{math|'''I'''}}, then the [[subalgebra]]  <math>\{x \bold I + y \bold A: x y \in \R\}</math> [[generator (mathematics)|generated by]] {{math|'''A'''}} is [[isomorphic]] to the [[split-complex number]]s.

If {{math|'''A'''}} and {{math|'''B'''}} are two involutory matrices which [[commuting matrices|commute]] with each other (i.e. {{math|1='''AB''' = '''BA'''}}) then {{math|'''AB'''}} is also involutory.

If {{math|'''A'''}} is an involutory matrix then every [[integer]] [[Matrix multiplication#Powers of a matrix|power]] of {{math|'''A'''}} is involutory. In fact, {{math|'''A'''<sup>''n''</sup>}} will be equal to {{math|'''A'''}} if {{mvar|n}} is [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] and {{math|'''I'''}} if {{mvar|n}} is [[parity (mathematics)|even]].
